quests.correctSentence: The meeting starts at 9 o'clock sharp.
quests.contrastSentence: The meeting starts on 9 o'clock sharp.
quests.ruleExplanation: 'At' is used for exact clock times: at 9 o'clock, at noon. 'On' is for days and dates, and 'in' is for longer periods like months or years.
quests.nativeTip: This is a specific point on the clock.

quests.correctSentence: Her birthday is in March, I think.
quests.contrastSentence: Her birthday is at March, I think.
quests.ruleExplanation: 'In' is used for months, years, and seasons: in March, in 2020, in summer. This is a longer period than the exact points that take 'at'.
quests.nativeTip: Months, like years, take the same preposition.

quests.correctSentence: — When's the party? — It's on Saturday evening.
quests.contrastSentence: — When's the party? — It's at Saturday evening.
quests.ruleExplanation: 'On' is used for specific days and dates: on Saturday, on July 4th. Even 'Saturday evening' as a whole phrase still takes 'on' because the day anchors it.
quests.nativeTip: Days of the week follow their own rule, different from clock times or months.

quests.correctSentence: I've lived in this city for five years.
quests.contrastSentence: I've lived in this city since five years.
quests.ruleExplanation: 'For' introduces a duration, a length of time: for five years, for two hours. 'Since' would instead point to when the period began.
quests.nativeTip: This word introduces a length of time, not a starting point.

quests.conceptTitle: Prepositions of Time: Since + Starting Point
quests.grammarRule: Prepositions of Time: Since + Starting Point
quests.correctSentence: I've lived in this city since 2019.
quests.contrastSentence: I've lived in this city for 2019.
quests.ruleExplanation: 'Since' introduces a specific starting point in time: since 2019, since last week. This contrasts directly with 'for', which describes duration instead.
quests.nativeTip: 2019 is a starting point, not a length of time.

quests.correctSentence: — When do you need this done? — By Friday, at the latest.
quests.contrastSentence: — When do you need this done? — Until Friday, at the latest.
quests.ruleExplanation: 'By' marks a deadline: by Friday means no later than Friday. 'Until' would describe something continuing up to that point, not a finishing deadline.
quests.nativeTip: This word marks a deadline — the latest possible moment for something to happen.

quests.correctSentence: The bakery is opposite the bank, right across the street.
quests.contrastSentence: The bakery is between the bank, right across the street.
quests.ruleExplanation: 'Opposite' describes something directly facing another single thing, often across a street: opposite the bank. 'Between' would need two reference points, not just one.
quests.nativeTip: Only one other place is mentioned, and it's on the other side of the street.

quests.correctSentence: She felt nervous among so many strangers.
quests.contrastSentence: She felt nervous between so many strangers.
quests.ruleExplanation: 'Among' is used for a position within a larger group of three or more: among strangers, among the crowd. 'Between' is reserved for exactly two people or things.
quests.nativeTip: This describes being surrounded by more than two people.

quests.correctSentence: — Is the pharmacy far from here? — No, it's near the corner, very close.
quests.contrastSentence: — Is the pharmacy far from here? — No, it's opposite the corner, very close.
quests.ruleExplanation: 'Near' simply describes short distance: near the corner. The answer 'very close' directly confirms this is the right word.
quests.nativeTip: The reply already tells you the distance is short.

quests.correctSentence: She walked into the room and sat down quietly.
quests.contrastSentence: She walked onto the room and sat down quietly.
quests.ruleExplanation: 'Into' describes movement that ends inside an enclosed space: walked into the room. 'Through' would suggest passing all the way across it and out the other side.
quests.nativeTip: She is entering an enclosed space, ending up inside it.

quests.correctSentence: The cat jumped onto the table and knocked over a cup.
quests.contrastSentence: The cat jumped into the table and knocked over a cup.
quests.ruleExplanation: 'Onto' describes movement ending on top of a surface: jumped onto the table. 'Into' would only fit if the table were a container the cat entered.
quests.nativeTip: The cat ends up on top of a surface, not inside anything.

quests.correctSentence: — How did you get to the other side of the river? — I walked across the bridge.
quests.contrastSentence: — How did you get to the other side of the river? — I walked into the bridge.
quests.ruleExplanation: 'Across' describes movement from one side of something to the other: walked across the bridge. 'Along' would instead describe moving lengthwise beside the river, not crossing it.
quests.nativeTip: This movement goes from one side to the other.

quests.correctSentence: I'm really interested in learning Spanish this year.
quests.contrastSentence: I'm really interested on learning Spanish this year.
quests.ruleExplanation: 'Interested' is always followed by 'in': interested in something. These fixed adjective-preposition pairs don't follow a general rule and need to be learned individually.
quests.nativeTip: This adjective always pairs with the same one preposition, and it must simply be memorized.

quests.correctSentence: She's afraid of spiders, even small ones.
quests.contrastSentence: She's afraid from spiders, even small ones.
quests.ruleExplanation: 'Afraid' always pairs with 'of': afraid of spiders, afraid of the dark. Like 'interested in', this combination simply has to be memorized as a fixed pair.
quests.nativeTip: This adjective has its own fixed partner preposition too.

quests.correctSentence: — Are you good at math? — Not really, I prefer art.
quests.contrastSentence: — Are you good for math? — Not really, I prefer art.
quests.ruleExplanation: 'Good' pairs with 'at' when talking about skill or ability: good at math, good at cooking. This is different from 'good for', which describes something being beneficial.
quests.nativeTip: This describes a skill or ability, which uses its own fixed preposition.

quests.correctSentence: This decision depends on the budget we're given.
quests.contrastSentence: This decision depends of the budget we're given.
quests.ruleExplanation: 'Depend' always takes 'on': depends on the budget. Like adjective-preposition pairs, verb-preposition pairs like this one need to be memorized as whole units.
quests.nativeTip: This verb always pairs with the same fixed preposition.

quests.correctSentence: Can you listen to me for just a second?
quests.contrastSentence: Can you listen at me for just a second?
quests.ruleExplanation: 'Listen' always pairs with 'to': listen to me, listen to music. This differs from 'look', which pairs with 'at' instead.
quests.nativeTip: This is one of the most common verb-preposition pairs in everyday English.

quests.correctSentence: — Are you waiting for someone? — Yes, my sister should be here any minute.
quests.contrastSentence: — Are you waiting to someone? — Yes, my sister should be here any minute.
quests.ruleExplanation: 'Wait' always pairs with 'for': waiting for someone, waiting for the bus. This is another fixed verb-preposition combination worth memorizing as a set.
quests.nativeTip: This verb pairs with the preposition that also introduces a reason or purpose.

quests.correctSentence: She sings beautifully ; the whole audience was silent.
quests.contrastSentence: She sings beautiful ; the whole audience was silent.
quests.ruleExplanation: Manner adverbs are usually formed by adding '-ly' to the adjective: beautiful → beautifully. 'Beautiful' alone describes a noun, not the way an action is performed.
quests.nativeTip: This word describes how she sings, so it needs the adverb form, not the adjective.

quests.correctSentence: He solved the problem easily , without any help.
quests.contrastSentence: He solved the problem easyly , without any help.
quests.ruleExplanation: Adjectives ending in -y change to -ily for the adverb form: easy → easily, happy → happily. 'Easyly' isn't correct spelling.
quests.nativeTip: This adjective ends in -y, which changes before the ending is added.

quests.correctSentence: — How did she do on the test? — She did well , actually — top of the class.
quests.contrastSentence: — How did she do on the test? — She did good , actually — top of the class.
quests.ruleExplanation: 'Good' has an irregular adverb form: well, not 'goodly'. Since this describes how she did (an action), the adverb 'well' is needed, not the adjective 'good'.
quests.nativeTip: This describes how she performed, and its adverb form is completely irregular.

quests.correctSentence: He is a good singer; everyone loves his voice.
quests.contrastSentence: He is a well singer; everyone loves his voice.
quests.ruleExplanation: 'Good' is an adjective, used to describe nouns: a good singer. 'Well' would only be used to describe how an action is performed, not to describe a person directly.
quests.nativeTip: This word describes the noun 'singer', not an action.

quests.correctSentence: He sings well ; that's why he joined the choir.
quests.contrastSentence: He sings good ; that's why he joined the choir.
quests.ruleExplanation: 'Well' is the adverb form, describing how the action of singing is performed: sings well. This contrasts directly with 'a good singer' from the last question, which described the noun instead.
quests.nativeTip: This word describes the action 'sings', not a noun.

quests.correctSentence: — Can you travel tomorrow? — Not yet, I'm not well enough.
quests.contrastSentence: — Can you travel tomorrow? — Not yet, I'm not good enough.
quests.ruleExplanation: 'Well' can also function as an adjective describing health: not well enough, feeling well. This is a special exception to the usual good/well adjective-adverb pattern.
quests.nativeTip: This describes a state of health, a special use of this particular word.

quests.correctSentence: We arrived at the airport just in time for the flight.
quests.contrastSentence: We arrived at the airport just on time for the flight.
quests.ruleExplanation: 'In time' is a fixed expression meaning arriving before a deadline, without being late: just in time. Neither 'on time' (arriving exactly when expected) nor 'at time' fits this specific phrase.
quests.nativeTip: This fixed phrase means 'not too late'.

quests.correctSentence: She explained the instructions very clearly , so no one was confused.
quests.contrastSentence: She explained the instructions very clear , so no one was confused.
quests.ruleExplanation: 'Clearly' is the adverb form of 'clear', describing how the explaining was done: explained clearly. 'Clear' alone would describe a noun, not an action.
quests.nativeTip: This describes how she explained, so it needs the adverb form.

quests.correctSentence: — Is the store open on Sundays? — No, only on weekdays.
quests.contrastSentence: — Is the store open at Sundays? — No, only on weekdays.
quests.ruleExplanation: 'On' is used for specific days, as reviewed back in Level 61: open on Sundays. The reply confirms this by also using 'on weekdays'.
quests.nativeTip: Days of the week keep the same preposition rule from Level 61.

quests.correctSentence: Please arrive at 8 am sharp; the doors close right after.
quests.contrastSentence: Please arrive on 8 am sharp; the doors close right after.
quests.ruleExplanation: Exact clock times take 'at': at 8 am. This is the same rule practiced at the very start of this stage, now appearing in a real workplace instruction.
quests.nativeTip: This is an exact clock time, just like Level 61.

quests.correctSentence: Please read the instructions carefully before you begin.
quests.contrastSentence: Please read the instructions careful before you begin.
quests.ruleExplanation: Since this describes the manner of reading, the adverb 'carefully' is needed, not the adjective 'careful'. This is common in real instructions and notices.
quests.nativeTip: This describes how the reading should be done.

quests.correctSentence: — Did you finish the report? — Yes, and I think I did it pretty well .
quests.contrastSentence: — Did you finish the report? — Yes, and I think I did it pretty good .
quests.ruleExplanation: This closes Stage 4 by returning to the good/well contrast from Level 68: since this describes how the work was performed, the adverb 'well' is correct, not 'good'.
quests.nativeTip: This describes how the report was done, just like Level 68.
